intro: This guide takes your group through Foxe’s Book of Martyrs (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter each week. It’s written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. John Foxe collected the true stories of Christians who suffered and died for their faith, and this edition retells some of the best known: Polycarp, Perpetua and Blandina, Wycliffe, Hus, Luther, Tyndale, Lady Jane Grey, Ridley and Latimer, Cranmer, persecuted Quakers and Adoniram and Ann Judson. It is honest, too, that Protestants persecuted others as well.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand. Talk it through using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about 10 minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper, pens and Bibles. These are stories of martyrdom, and many end in death by fire, hanging or the arena. The edition avoids gory detail, so don’t add it; keep the focus on courage, faith and forgiveness. Some teens will be troubled by the violence, and some may worry about whether they would be brave enough, so remind them that the martyrs were often frightened and found strength by God’s grace. Handle Chapter 11 carefully, with respect for Christians of every tradition, and if anyone in your group has faced bullying or hostility for their faith, follow up with them privately.

weeks.summary: John Foxe fled England in 1554 when Queen Mary began persecuting Protestants, and in exile he gathered letters, trial records and last words of those who died for their faith, publishing them in a huge book. He built it on Jesus’ promise that the gates of hell would not prevail against his church: Christ would have a church, it would be attacked, and it would continue. The chapter also prepares readers for hard stories told honestly, including times Protestants persecuted others. The big idea: the church has been fiercely attacked but never destroyed, because Christ keeps his promise.

memory_verse.text: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

activity.title: Stephen’s Story
steps: Read Acts 7:54–60 aloud together.
In small groups, have teens note what Stephen saw, what he said, and how he prayed for the people killing him.
Discuss: how does Stephen’s death fit Foxe’s three points about the church: it exists, it is attacked, and it continues?
Ask what they expect to find hard about reading true stories that end in death, and what they hope to learn.
Encourage everyone to read the whole of Acts 6:8–7:60 at home this week.

weeks.summary: Polycarp, the elderly bishop of Smyrna, is tracked down and arrested, gives his captors a meal and asks for an hour to pray, praying so fervently that his guards feel ashamed. Told by the governor to curse Christ and go free, he answers that he has served Christ eighty-six years and never been wronged, so how can he blaspheme his King? He is put to death, but his words outlive the empire. The big idea: courage in hard moments grows out of a long, real friendship with Jesus.

memory_verse.text: For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

activity.title: He Never Wronged Me
steps: Read Polycarp’s answer to the governor aloud.
Ask everyone to write, for themselves, three ways Jesus has been faithful to them so far.
Discuss: what small, everyday versions of Polycarp’s choice do teens face, where saying you follow Jesus costs something?
Talk about why Polycarp spoke about a relationship rather than giving a speech about doctrine.
Encourage everyone to keep their list somewhere they will see it and read it when following Jesus feels costly.

weeks.summary: Many martyrs were young: Perpetua, about twenty-two, died in Carthage alongside Felicitas, a pregnant young woman, and Revocatus, a slave, all treated as equals in Christ. In Lyons, frail Blandina encouraged others by her prayers and died with Ponticus, a boy of fifteen. The chapter points out that costly faith is not only for later in life. The big idea: young people can be examples of faith, and even the weak can strengthen others.

memory_verse.text: Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.

activity.title: Be a Blandina
steps: Read 1 Timothy 4:12 together and list the five areas Paul names: speech, conduct, love, faith and purity.
In pairs, have teens think of one realistic way someone their age could set an example in each area.
Share a few ideas as a group.
Discuss: Blandina was physically weak but strengthened others. What does encouragement look like between friends today?
Ask everyone to think privately of one friend who is finding faith hard, and to send them an encouraging message this week.

weeks.summary: In 1300s England most people could not read the Bible in their own language. John Wycliffe, an Oxford scholar, argued that the Bible should be the final authority, refused to recant when friars came to his sickbed, and set about translating the Bible into English, copied by hand. His followers, the Lollards, were persecuted, and he became known as “the Morning Star of the Reformation.” The big idea: God’s word in our own language is a costly gift, and it gives light.

memory_verse.text: The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple.

activity.title: A Bible Copied by Hand
steps: Give everyone a short passage, such as Psalm 23, and ask them to copy it out by hand as neatly as they can.
After a few minutes, stop and ask how long a whole Gospel or a whole Bible would take at that speed.
Discuss what it would be like to hear the Bible only in a language you didn’t understand.
Ask: how easy is it to take the Bible for granted when you can find it on your phone in seconds?
Challenge everyone to read a chapter every day this week, thanking God first that they can read it in their own language.

weeks.summary: Jan Hus, a pastor in Prague inspired by Wycliffe, preached in the people’s language and spoke against corruption. Promised safe travel to the Council of Constance, he was arrested instead, condemned, and refused to take back his teaching. Before he died he said his Lord had worn a harder chain, and that they were burning a goose but a swan would follow, which later readers linked to Martin Luther. The big idea: you can kill a messenger, but you cannot kill the truth he carries.

memory_verse.text: And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.

activity.title: Saying It Kindly
steps: Read Hus’s words about the “rusty” chain aloud.
Ask everyone to write down privately one true thing about Jesus that they find hard to say around certain people.
In pairs, have teens practise saying a true, simple sentence about their faith in a kind and natural way, using a made-up everyday situation.
Discuss what made Hus unafraid, and what Jesus means about not fearing those who can only kill the body.
Challenge everyone to look for one natural opportunity this week to say something true about Jesus, kindly and honestly.

weeks.summary: Martin Luther came to believe from the Bible that we are made right with God by faith as a free gift, and spoke against selling forgiveness. Summoned before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and told to take back his books, he said he would change his mind if shown wrong from Scripture, but his conscience was bound by God’s word. Declared an outlaw, he was hidden by friends and translated the New Testament into German. The big idea: stand firm where God’s word stands, and be humble enough to be corrected by it.

memory_verse.text: But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.”

activity.title: Conscience or Feelings?
steps: Read Luther’s answer at Worms aloud.
Write two headings on a board: “Tied by the Scriptures” and “Just my feelings.”
Read out several made-up situations where someone takes a stand, and sort them together under the two headings.
Discuss why Luther said he would change his mind if shown wrong from the Bible, and why that makes his stand stronger, not weaker.
Ask everyone to think privately of one area where they feel pressure to go along with something wrong, and to look up what the Bible says about it this week.

weeks.summary: William Tyndale vowed to make a ploughboy know more Scripture than a churchman who preferred the pope’s laws to God’s. Working in hiding abroad, he translated the New Testament from Greek into clear English, and copies were smuggled into England. Betrayed and imprisoned, he impressed even his guards, and he died praying, “Lord! open the king of England’s eyes.” Within a few years an English Bible, much of it his, was placed in every church. The big idea: the Bible in our hands was costly, and the best way to honour that is to read it.

memory_verse.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

activity.title: The Ploughboy Challenge
steps: Read Tyndale’s vow about the boy who drives the plough aloud.
As a group, list short books of the Bible that could be read in a week, such as Mark, James, Philippians or 1 John.
Ask everyone to choose one book they have never read all the way through.
Discuss: Tyndale’s last words were a prayer for the king who opposed him. What does that show about him?
Challenge everyone to read their chosen book through this week, a little each day.

weeks.summary: Lady Jane Grey, about sixteen, was pushed onto the throne for nine days and then condemned when Mary became queen. Offered her life if she gave up her faith, she refused, and on the scaffold she said she looked to be saved only by God’s mercy in the blood of Jesus, honestly confessed her own failings, prayed Psalm 51 and willingly forgave her executioner. The big idea: our only hope is God’s mercy in Christ, and his mercy makes us able to forgive.

memory_verse.text: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions.

activity.title: Only by Mercy
steps: Read Jane’s words on the scaffold aloud.
Ask the group to list things people today might rely on to feel right with God, such as family, learning, being good or going to church.
Compare that list with Jane’s hope: “only by the mercy of God in the blood of His only Son Jesus Christ.”
Discuss why forgiving someone who hurts you is so hard, and how Jesus’ forgiveness makes it possible.
Ask everyone to write down privately the name of someone they need to forgive, and to ask God for help with it this week.

weeks.summary: Under Queen Mary hundreds were burned for their faith, among them Nicholas Ridley and the elderly preacher Hugh Latimer, who died together in Oxford in 1555. As the fire was lit, Latimer encouraged his nervous friend to be brave, trusting that by God’s grace they would light a candle in England that would never be put out. Ridley, at the end, pleaded for some poor tenants. The big idea: Christians are lights in dark times, and they hold each other up by God’s grace.

memory_verse.text: You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.

activity.title: Be Someone’s Latimer
steps: Read Latimer’s words to Ridley aloud.
Discuss the two things the chapter notices: Latimer encouraged his friend, and he relied on God’s grace rather than his own bravery.
In pairs, have teens write a short, sincere message of encouragement they could send to a Christian friend going through a hard time.
Talk about the small ways teens can be light at school or online.
Encourage everyone to send a message like that to a real friend this week.

weeks.summary: Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, was imprisoned and, frightened, was pressured step by step into signing papers denying everything he had taught. Brought to read his denial in public, he instead took it all back, and at the stake held his right hand into the fire first, crying, “This unworthy right hand,” before dying with Stephen’s prayer. The big idea: failure is not the end; God forgives those who turn back to him.

memory_verse.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

activity.title: Step by Step
steps: Read the description of how Cranmer was pressured to sign one paper after another.
Discuss how pressure often works in small steps, and list some everyday examples together without anyone sharing their own story.
Talk about Peter, who denied Jesus and was restored, and how Cranmer’s story ends.
Ask everyone to write down privately one time they gave in to pressure, then to bring it to God in silence and receive his forgiveness.
Close by reading 1 John 1:9 together.

weeks.summary: The chapter shows that Protestants persecuted others too: Puritans in Boston, who had themselves fled persecution, passed harsh laws against Quakers and hanged William Robinson, Marmaduke Stevenson and Mary Dyer. Foxe himself begged Queen Elizabeth to spare two Anabaptists. The lessons are humility, the Golden Rule, and love for Christians of other traditions. The big idea: no group of Christians has a perfect record, and we must never use power to force anyone’s faith.

memory_verse.text: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

activity.title: Listening Across Traditions
steps: Read Foxe’s words: “I have no favour for heretics, but I am a man and would spare the life of a man.”
Discuss why people who suffered persecution sometimes became persecutors once they had power.
As a group, list Christian traditions the teens know of, such as Catholic, Orthodox and different Protestant churches.
In pairs, write three respectful questions they could ask a Christian from a different tradition about their faith.
Encourage everyone to pray this week for a Christian from another tradition by name, and if possible ask them one of those questions and listen.

weeks.summary: From a haystack prayer meeting of students in 1806 came the first American missionary society, and Adoniram and Ann Judson went to Burma, where they began translating the Bible. When war broke out Judson was imprisoned as a suspected spy, and Ann kept him alive, pleading with officials and caring for their baby while seriously ill herself. His Burmese New Testament survived, hidden in a hard pillow. The big idea: remember those imprisoned for their faith, and pray and help as if we were with them.

memory_verse.text: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.

activity.title: Remember Them
activity.materials: Paper and pens, and if possible a phone or laptop
steps: Read the description of Judson’s translation being hidden in a hard pillow.
Ask the group to name countries where they think Christians face persecution today, and if you have a device, look up one together using a reliable Christian charity’s website.
Write down three specific things to pray for the Christians in that country.
Spend a few minutes praying together for them.
Discuss how your group or church might support those who help persecuted Christians, and pick one idea to follow up.

weeks.summary: The final chapter gathers the whole book: an old bishop, young believers, translators, a teenage queen, friends at the stake, an archbishop who fell and stood again, persecuted Quakers and missionaries in prison. Hebrews calls them a great cloud of witnesses cheering on the runners who follow. Their lessons: courage comes from relationship, God’s word is worth everything, failure is not the end, be honest about our own side, and above all Jesus is worth it. The big idea: we run our own race with our eyes on Jesus, surrounded by those who went before.

memory_verse.text: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us.

activity.title: My Witness
steps: Read the five lessons from the chapter aloud.
Ask everyone to choose the one story from the whole book that moved them most.
Go round the group and let each person who wishes name their story and say in a sentence why.
Give everyone a few minutes to write a short prayer asking God for the same faith.
Encourage them to pray it every day this week.
